parsed.thesis: An owner's explicit approval of an artifact is the strongest available signal of intent and must be converted into an immutable anchor before any further iteration. Improvement should proceed only as reversible experiments measured against that anchor, with success defined by observable comparative evidence of non-regression rather than by completion of the edit action itself; and when 'better' remains undefined, clarification and restraint take precedence over autonomous open-ended optimization.

principleCandidate.title: Anchor iteration to the owner-approved baseline with evidence-gated, reversible changes
principleCandidate.rationale: The failure compounded because approval was treated as transient: each degraded round became the next round's starting point, 'success' meant having performed the edit, and 'better' was never defined. Freezing the approved state as an immutable reference, experimenting only on copies, and gating every change on observable non-regression versus that reference breaks the drift chain at its root and makes degradation detectable at the gate instead of after multiple stacked rounds.
principleCandidate.scope: Any iterative refinement of an artifact the owner has explicitly approved or accepted (media, documents, code, generated outputs, configurations), especially when quality is subjective, the optimization target is underspecified, and changes would otherwise stack directly on the live artifact.

risks: Overlaps with existing core axioms: it largely operationalizes T-02 (approved state as explicit intent signal), T-03 (observable evidence before claiming results), T-04 (reversible actions), and T-07 (verify against intended outcome); its distinct contribution is only the composite pattern of freezing approval as an immutable comparison anchor.
Baseline fixation: an agent may resist or slow-walk legitimate new directions from the owner; the anchor must be re-baselined whenever the owner issues a new explicit approval or revised goal.
Comparison evidence (e.g., keyframe screenshots, clip diffs) may not fully capture subjective quality, creating false confidence in acceptance gates and wrongly rejecting or accepting changes.
Generating per-round comparison evidence and version history adds time and storage cost; for trivial low-stakes edits this can become over-engineering and delay delivery.
Clarification-first stance may degrade into excessive questioning when the owner expects autonomy; the fallback should be minimal intervention on the anchor, not stalling.

parsed.thesis: Once an owner explicitly approves a deliverable, that approval becomes the objective anchor of quality. Iteration that drifts from this anchor—driven by self-assessed improvements, unverified by observable comparison, ungated by non-degradation checks, and unrecoverable via rollback—silently accumulates degradation while each round reports success. Iteration discipline is defined not by completing changes, but by proving each change is no worse than the state the owner already accepted.

principleCandidate.rationale: The root cause of the pain was unanchored subjective iteration: vague 'optimize' requests were treated as license for self-judged modification, with no fixed reference version, no comparative acceptance evidence, and no prohibition on carrying degraded versions forward as new starting points. principleDraft.title: Anchor iterative refinement on owner-approved baselines with non-regression verification
principleDraft.statement: When an owner has explicitly approved a version of an artifact whose quality is judged by preference, that version must be fixed as the iteration baseline before any further modification: record its identifier and reference evidence, keep each change reversible from that baseline, accept a change only after an observable side-by-side comparison against the baseline, roll back any change that degrades relative quality, and never promote a degraded version as the starting point for the next round.
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was unanchored subjective iteration: a vague 'optimize' request was treated as license for self-judged modification with no fixed reference version, no comparative acceptance evidence, and no prohibition on carrying degraded versions forward, so each round compounded drift while the agent believed it was improving. Anchoring on the owner-approved version converts 'better' from agent self-judgment into a verifiable relative judgment, and the non-regression-plus-rollback rule blocks the compounding of errors across rounds.
applicability: Iterative refinement of artifacts whose quality is judged by owner preference or subjective standards — video, images, audio, documents, UI, generated creative content
Follow-up modification requests issued after the owner has explicitly approved a specific version, especially vague ones such as 'optimize', 'improve', 'adjust', 'make it better'
Multi-round modification workflows where no acceptance criteria have been re-established for the new rounds
antiPatterns: Treating a vague 'optimize' request as license for self-judged modification without recording the owner-approved version as the reference
Declaring a modification round successful upon completion alone, without observable comparison evidence against the baseline
Retaining a change that observably degrades relative to the baseline, or using a degraded output as the starting point for the next iteration
Discarding or overwriting the owner-approved baseline without a recoverable copy, making rollback impossible
Substituting agent aesthetic self-assessment for owner approval as the acceptance standard

intentContract.targetBehavior: Upon receiving a follow-up modification request for an owner-approved artifact, the agent first records the approved version as baseline (identifier plus reference evidence such as keyframe screenshots), then after each change produces an observable side-by-side comparison against that baseline, keeps the change only if it is no worse, and otherwise rolls back to the baseline and starts the next round from it.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Unanchored subjective iteration: performing self-judged 'optimization' rounds with no recorded owner-approved baseline, declaring each round successful on completion alone, and carrying degraded versions forward as iteration starting points so degradation compounds — the 'each round worse than the approved version, getting messier' failure family.
intentContract.evidenceSource: The owner's direct correction that all later 'optimizations' were worse than the approved mooncake-mv-final-v3k22.mp4 ('后面的所谓的优化都没有 mooncake-mv-final-v3k22.mp4 版本好，越搞越乱'), recorded as a severe user_correction pain and diagnosed (diagnosis_pain_host_cffdcb9f5d02576d1e211436008f124778b4564fb1cf0230cc96ef03faf0c2f1) as missing baseline anchoring, comparative acceptance evidence, and a non-degradation guardrail.
intentContract.validationExpectation: A rule is faithful only if it (a) triggers on modification requests that follow an owner-approved version, (b) requires baseline recording (identifier plus reference evidence) before changes, (c) requires observable comparison evidence against the baseline before a change is retained, and (d) mandates rollback and forbids promoting degraded outputs to the iteration baseline; a rule that merely says 'verify improvements' or 'ask the owner' without baseline anchoring and non-regression does not satisfy this intent.

risks: This principle is a synthesis that overlaps existing core axioms — T-02 (owner approval as intent anchor), T-03 (observable comparative evidence), T-04/T-05 (rollback and forbidden degrading transitions), T-07 (verified success); its novelty is the composite baseline-anchoring-plus-non-regression workflow, so rule generation must avoid emitting rules that duplicate axiom-level guidance

Over-conservative anchoring: if the owner's intent genuinely evolves or the baseline itself is flawed, a frozen baseline becomes a stale constraint contradicting T-02; the principle must allow re-anchoring when the owner approves a new version or explicitly changes direction
Mandating per-round comparison evidence adds cost and latency; for trivial or precisely specified changes this can become bureaucratic overhead conflicting with the simplicity intent of T-06

'Degradation' on subjective qualities remains ambiguous without owner-clarified criteria — the agent may over-ask (friction) or fall back to self-judgment (drift); the source diagnosis itself carried low confidence (0.55) with missing agent-side tool-trajectory evidence, so the non-regression boundary may be hard to operationalize
